author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper: https://tedd.or
summary: Barton summarizes Grossman et al.'s comparative case-study of eight professional-education programs across three fields — clergy training, clinical psychology, and teaching — examining how each profession teaches the pedagogy of practice itself. The researchers analyzed site visits, interviews, observations, and focus groups to build a shared framework of three concepts: representations, decomposition, and approximations of practice. Their central finding is that prospective teachers get markedly fewer opportunities than trainee clergy or psychologists to engage in approximations of interactive practice — the low-stakes rehearsal of in-the-moment demands like responding to questions or handling resistance. Barton notes the framework's purpose is to give teacher educators a common vocabulary for analyzing and improving how practice is taught, not just what content is taught. His key-implications section argues that decomposing practice into visible components builds professional vision, while approximating practice lets trainees experiment and falter safely before facing real classroom stakes.
points: Decomposing practice into visible components makes the “grammar of practice” explicit, helping trainee teachers develop professional vision and a shared language for analyzing their own performance.
Approximations of practice — deliberate, low-stakes rehearsal of a specific skill — let trainees experiment and receive feedback without risking a live classroom.

Teacher preparation programs give trainees far fewer opportunities to practice interactive skills (responding to questions, orchestrating discussion, handling resistance) than clergy or clinical-psychology programs give their trainees.
Artificial, decontextualized practice settings have real pedagogical value: isolating one element of a complex skill lets novices hone it before juggling the full complexity of live practice.
quotes: Decomposing practice makes visible the "grammar of practice," enabling teachers to understand and enact essential elements of practice more effectively.
Approximating practice allows teachers to engage in "deliberate practice" of challenging components of practice in a safe space, with opportunities to experiment, falter, and receive feedback.
Classroom approximations of practice can help teachers avoid predictable errors in the field by providing opportunities to practice high-stakes interactions in low-risk environments.
The study finds that prospective teachers have fewer opportunities to engage in approximations of interactive practice compared to novices in the other two professions.
The artifice involved in such examples of the teaching of practice affords unique learning opportunities for novices.

The focus on components of complex practice allows students to hone their skills in a single element of reading, therapy, preaching, or worship before they have to manage all the competing demands and conditions of uncertainty in actual practice
